doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Monk, the Army and learning the job
title: Army, Columbia, The Record Changer and meeting Monk at Alfred Lion's
summary: After the Army he returned to Columbia, edited The Record Changer with Bill Grauer, and met Monk at the Lions' home.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Fine. Okay. The world has gone on to other forms of waylaying people. I mean I’m not old enough to have been around when the press gangs were kidnapping sailors and putting them on ships in the harbor, but this is almost it. But no the point is so what I’m saying is it’s a combination of a certain amount of osmosis. Pop music was in the air to a very large extent and it was very close to being or actually was jazz at this point, and then also physical circumstances made it possible for me to have direct listening experience even though it wasn’t an overwhelming love of music maybe that led me in there in the first place. But I heard it, I listened to it, so that by the time I got into the Army, which was when I was about like just short of being 21 when I got into the armed forces, I was sufficiently immersed in music at a time that, just a couple of years ago when a guy that I had been hanging out with a good deal in those days, in my Army days we lost sight of each other for decades and then re-encountered each other and we were reminiscing, actually strictly by mail, he lives in Europe now, but reminiscing about the old days and the thing that had been the first bond between us was the mutual love of the Ellington band. So that I was sufficiently into it. Then when I came out of the Army and went — my family was living in the immediate vicinity of Columbia University. I had graduated from Columbia. And I went back in the general campus area, after being in the armed forces I felt I had three years of total illiteracy. I had been an English major. I intended to go into some form of writing or publishing or whatnot, and I felt that I needed a kind of a crash course in being literate again. So I went back on campus, got into the graduate English school and wasn’t looking for a degree, didn’t stay there that long, but by doing that there was a group of people who I had known, not necessarily all that well but who I had known in the pre-war period which included Bill Grauer, who in the late 40s took over as publisher of a very esoteric jazz magazine called The Record Changer which basically it survived on the basis of having in its columns mail order buying, selling and auctioning of rare 78 old jazz records. And at that point I had gotten what I considered the proper kind of job for me, I was a young editor in a book publishing house. I like to say I worked at Simon & Schuster so long ago that I worked for Mr. Simon and Mr. Schuster and I really did. But I had this relationship going with — a working scene going with Grauer, for example, and I became editor of that publication. And among the things that happened early on was that Bill and I were invited down to the Greenwich Village home of Alfred and Lorraine Lion, because Alfred had just started to push Blue Note into modern jazz and we were claiming that The Record Changer would be open to considering all kinds of jazz, not just the traditional which it had previously been involved with. And so we were invited down there to meet and to listen to test pressings from the first recording session for Blue Note of Thelonious Monk. I was so damn dumb
